dx: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis with large-vessel involvement
case: A 74-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of new right-sided headache, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness. Twice this week she has had transient blurred vision in the right eye. She also has aching and morning stiffness of both shoulders. Physical examination shows a thickened, tender right superficial temporal artery with a diminished pulse. Blood pressure is 142/80 mm Hg in the right arm and 118/74 mm Hg in the left arm. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 88 mm/h (less than 42 for her age and sex) and a C-reactive protein concentration of 64 mg/L (less than 10). Temporal artery biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation of the media with multinucleated giant cells and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina. Diagnosis: giant cell (temporal) arteritis.

questions.stem: Permanent vision loss in this disease most often results from occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries, which supply the optic nerve head. These arteries are branches of an artery that arises from which of the following vessels?
options: Internal carotid artery
External carotid artery
Superficial temporal artery
Basilar artery
approach: Key clue: one-eye vision loss from ischemia of the optic nerve head.
The posterior ciliary arteries are branches of the ophthalmic artery.
The ophthalmic artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery, so the eye is fed by a different carotid system than the scalp and jaw.
questions.why: Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is the usual cause of blindness in giant cell arteritis. It results from inflammatory occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries, which come off the ophthalmic artery. The ophthalmic artery is the first major branch of the internal carotid artery after it leaves the cavernous sinus. The biopsied superficial temporal artery belongs to the external carotid system, so this disease can threaten both carotid territories at once.
whyNot: Correct.

The external carotid artery supplies the scalp, face, and chewing muscles through branches such as the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries. It explains her scalp tenderness and jaw claudication, while the optic nerve head is supplied from the internal carotid system.
The superficial temporal artery is the inflamed artery that was biopsied. It is a terminal branch of the external carotid and does not give rise to the vessels that feed the eye.

The basilar artery supplies the brainstem and, through the posterior cerebral arteries, the occipital cortex. Vision loss from that system affects the visual fields of both eyes, while her symptoms are in one eye.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate?
options: Hemoglobin polymerizes and makes the red cells rigid and sickle shaped
Red cells gain water and swell into spheres that resist stacking
Fibrinogen masks red cell surface charge, letting cells form rouleaux
Albumin binds red cells and adds to their mutual surface repulsion
approach: Key clue: ESR rises in inflammation, so the change must come from acute-phase proteins.
IL-6 drives the liver to make fibrinogen, the main plasma protein that speeds sedimentation.
Fibrinogen lowers the negative-charge repulsion between red cells, so they stack and fall faster.
questions.why: IL-6 from the inflamed arteries signals hepatocytes to make acute-phase proteins, chiefly fibrinogen. Red cells normally carry a negative surface charge (the zeta potential) that keeps them apart. Large, asymmetric plasma proteins such as fibrinogen reduce this repulsion, so red cells stack into rouleaux. A stack has more mass for its surface area than a single cell, so it falls faster and the ESR rises.
whyNot: Sickled cells are rigid and cannot form rouleaux, so sickle cell anemia tends to give a low ESR. Polymerization of hemoglobin S also has no link to inflammation.
Spherocytes stack poorly, so swollen spherical cells lower the ESR, as in hereditary spherocytosis.
Correct.
Albumin opposes rouleaux formation, so a high albumin tends to slow the ESR and a low albumin speeds it. It cannot explain a high ESR in active inflammation.

questions.stem: She also reports aching and fatigue of the left arm when she carries groceries. Imaging shows narrowing of the artery that continues as the left axillary artery. This narrowed artery arises from which of the following?
options: Brachiocephalic trunk
Arch of the aorta
Left common carotid artery
Thyrocervical trunk
approach: Key clue: lower left arm pressure plus arm claudication means a stenosis upstream of the left axillary artery.
The artery that becomes the axillary artery is the subclavian artery.
The left subclavian is the third branch of the aortic arch; the right subclavian comes from the brachiocephalic trunk.
questions.why: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib. On the left, the subclavian artery arises directly from the arch of the aorta as its third branch, after the brachiocephalic trunk and the left common carotid artery. Giant cell arteritis involves the aorta and its main branches in a sizable share of patients, and subclavian narrowing gives arm claudication and unequal arm pressures, as in this woman.
whyNot: The brachiocephalic trunk gives rise to the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries. It would be the answer for a narrowing that lowered pressure in the right arm.
Correct.
The left common carotid artery is the second arch branch and supplies the head and neck. It does not give rise to the artery of the arm.
The thyrocervical trunk is a branch of the subclavian artery, so it lies downstream of the narrowed vessel.

questions.stem: In this disease, adventitial dendritic cells present an unidentified antigen to CD4+ T lymphocytes, which then drive inflammation in the media. Which of the following T-lymphocyte responses is mainly responsible for the granulomatous inflammation in her artery wall?
options: Th2 cells releasing IL-4 and IL-5 that recruit eosinophils
CD8 T cells releasing perforin and granzymes that kill endothelial cells
Regulatory T cells releasing IL-10 that quiets macrophages
Th1 cells releasing interferon gamma that activates macrophages
approach: Key clue: the biopsy shows granulomas with multinucleated giant cells and no mention of eosinophils or immune complexes.
Granulomas are a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity pattern driven by CD4 T cells.
Th1 cells release interferon gamma, which activates macrophages that gather into granulomas and fuse into giant cells.
questions.why: Giant cell arteritis is a T cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction in the artery wall. Activated dendritic cells in the adventitia prime CD4 T cells, which polarize mainly to Th1 and Th17 cells. Interferon gamma from Th1 cells activates macrophages, which form granulomas, fuse into multinucleated giant cells, and release enzymes and growth factors. These damage the elastic laminae and cause intimal thickening that narrows the lumen and causes ischemia, as in her jaw and eye.
whyNot: Th2 cells and eosinophils drive allergic inflammation and the eosinophil-rich vasculitis of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which occurs with asthma. Her biopsy does not describe eosinophils.
CD8 T cells kill cells that display foreign peptide on MHC class I, as in viral infection and transplant rejection. Cytotoxic killing does not build granulomas.
Regulatory T cells and IL-10 suppress inflammation. Lack of them can allow autoimmunity, but they do not produce granulomas.
Correct.

dx: Secondary Raynaud phenomenon caused by systemic sclerosis
case: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 10-year history of episodes in which her fingers turn white, then blue, then red on exposure to cold or emotional stress. Over the past 3 years, the skin of her fingers and face has become thick and tight. She also has heartburn and a sensation of solid food sticking behind the sternum. Physical examination shows tight, shiny skin over the fingers distal to the metacarpophalangeal joints, with normal skin over the upper arms and trunk. There is a healing pitted ulcer on the right index fingertip, firm subcutaneous calcium deposits in two finger pads, and telangiectasias on the face and lips. Nailfold capillaroscopy shows enlarged capillary loops with areas of capillary dropout. Antinuclear antibody assay is positive. Diagnosis: secondary Raynaud phenomenon caused by systemic sclerosis.

questions.stem: During an attack, her fingers turn red as they rewarm after the blue phase. Which of the following best explains the red phase?
options: Increased sympathetic alpha-adrenergic tone in the digital arteries
Rising venous pressure that traps deoxygenated blood in the skin
Reactive hyperemia from local vasodilator metabolites
Polycythemia that raises the hemoglobin content of skin capillaries
approach: Match each color to blood flow: white is no flow, blue is slow flow with deoxygenated blood, red is flow returning.
During ischemia, metabolites build up in the tissue.
When the spasm ends, these metabolites dilate arterioles and flow overshoots: reactive hyperemia.
questions.why: The white phase is vasospasm of the digital arteries that stops flow. The blue phase follows as a small amount of slowly moving blood gives up its oxygen. While flow is low, vasodilator metabolites such as adenosine, carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions, and potassium build up in the tissue. When the spasm relaxes, these metabolites hold the arterioles open, and flow rises above its resting level. This overshoot, called reactive hyperemia, makes the fingers red and often throbbing.
whyNot: Sympathetic alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction triggered by cold or stress causes the white phase, not the red one.
Slow flow with deoxygenated blood in the skin explains the blue phase. The red phase means fresh arterial blood is flowing in again.
Correct.
Polycythemia can make skin look ruddy all the time, but it would not appear in a pattern that follows each cold attack. Her color change comes from a change in flow.

topics: Reactive hyperemia and local metabolic control

questions.stem: Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be found in her serum?
options: Anticentromere antibody
Anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody
Anti-Jo-1 antibody
Anti-double-stranded DNA antibody
approach: Key clue: skin thickening only on the fingers and face, with calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, and telangiectasias.
This pattern is the limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis (CREST).
Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is most strongly linked to anticentromere antibody.
questions.why: Her skin changes stop at the fingers and face, with calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias. These five features make up CREST syndrome, the limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis. Raynaud phenomenon often comes years before skin changes in this form, as it did for her. Anticentromere antibody is the autoantibody most closely tied to this form, which carries a later risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension.
whyNot: Correct.

Anti-Scl-70 is linked to diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis, in which skin thickening spreads to the upper arms and trunk and interstitial lung disease is common. Her trunk and upper arms are spared.
Anti-Jo-1 is a marker of inflammatory myositis (polymyositis or dermatomyositis), often with interstitial lung disease. She has no muscle weakness.
Anti-double-stranded DNA is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and tracks with lupus nephritis. It is not typical of systemic sclerosis.

questions.stem: The fibrosis in her skin and esophagus is driven largely by transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta), which stimulates fibroblasts to deposit excess collagen. Which of the following best describes how the TGF-beta receptor transmits this signal into the cell?
options: Activation of Gs, which raises cyclic AMP
Tyrosine autophosphorylation that recruits RAS
Associated JAK kinases that phosphorylate STAT proteins
Serine/threonine phosphorylation of SMAD proteins
approach: Identify the mediator: TGF-beta is the main profibrotic cytokine in systemic sclerosis.
Recall its receptor class: TGF-beta receptors are serine/threonine kinases.
The activated receptor phosphorylates SMAD proteins, which carry the signal to the nucleus.
questions.why: TGF-beta binds the type II receptor, a serine/threonine kinase, which then phosphorylates and activates the type I receptor. The type I receptor phosphorylates SMAD2 and SMAD3. These join SMAD4, move into the nucleus, and switch on genes for collagen and other matrix proteins. In systemic sclerosis, persistent TGF-beta signaling keeps fibroblasts producing matrix, which thickens the skin and stiffens the esophageal wall.
whyNot: Gs coupling and cyclic AMP are used by receptors such as the beta-adrenergic receptors and the glucagon receptor, not by TGF-beta receptors.
Tyrosine autophosphorylation and RAS recruitment describe receptor tyrosine kinases such as the receptors for insulin, EGF, and PDGF.
JAK-STAT signaling is used by many cytokine receptors, such as those for IL-6, interferons, and erythropoietin. TGF-beta uses SMAD proteins instead.
Correct.

questions.stem: Fingertip ulceration is rare in primary Raynaud phenomenon. Which of the following changes in her digital arteries best explains why her attacks cause tissue loss?
options: Immune complex leukocytoclastic vasculitis of postcapillary venules
Intimal proliferation and fibrosis that keep the lumen narrow
Cholesterol-rich atheroma with a thin fibrous cap
Cold-reacting IgM antibodies that agglutinate red cells in the fingers
approach: Compare primary and secondary Raynaud: primary is pure vasospasm in a normal vessel; secondary adds structural vessel disease.
In systemic sclerosis, endothelial injury leads to intimal proliferation and fibrosis of small arteries, and capillaries are lost (seen on nailfold capillaroscopy).
A vessel that is already narrow closes completely during spasm, so ischemia is deeper and lasts longer, causing ulcers.
questions.why: In primary Raynaud phenomenon the digital arteries are structurally normal, so blood flow returns fully after each spasm and ulcers are rare. In systemic sclerosis, endothelial injury triggers intimal proliferation and fibrosis of small arteries, and capillaries drop out, as her nailfold capillaroscopy shows. The lumen stays narrow between attacks, so each spasm shuts the vessel completely and ischemia lasts longer. The result is pitting scars, ulcers, and sometimes gangrene of the fingertips.
whyNot: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis from immune complexes affects postcapillary venules and gives palpable purpura, as in IgA vasculitis or cryoglobulinemia. It does not explain cold-triggered digital ischemia.
Correct.
Atheroma forms mainly in large and medium arteries, not in small digital arteries, and it is not the lesion of systemic sclerosis.
Cold agglutinins cause acrocyanosis and hemolysis in cold exposure. They are not part of systemic sclerosis, and her antibody findings point to an autoimmune connective tissue disease.

case: A 36-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of cramping pain in the arch of his right foot when he walks. For the past 2 weeks he has had pain in his right toes at rest that is worse at night. He has smoked about 30 cigarettes daily since the age of 15 years. Last year he had tender, erythematous cords along superficial veins of both forearms that resolved spontaneously. He does not have diabetes mellitus. Physical examination shows a small dry ulcer at the tip of the right great toe. Femoral and popliteal pulses are normal; the right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent. Serum LDL cholesterol concentration is 96 mg/dL (less than 100). Angiography shows segmental occlusions of the tibial arteries with corkscrew-shaped collateral vessels. Diagnosis: thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease).

questions.stem: A biopsy specimen of an involved segment of his tibial artery obtained during the acute phase is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells centered on the internal elastic lamina
Inflamed thrombus with microabscesses that spreads to the nearby vein and nerve
Lipid-rich atheroma with cholesterol clefts beneath a fibrous cap
Transmural fibrinoid necrosis with lesions at different stages of healing
approach: Key clues: young heavy smoker, distal small and medium arteries, migratory superficial thrombophlebitis, and normal lipids.
Buerger disease is a segmental inflammation of arteries, veins, and nerves of the limbs.
Its acute lesion is a cellular, inflamed thrombus with microabscesses, with inflammation that extends to the neighboring vein and nerve.
questions.why: Thromboangiitis obliterans is a segmental, thrombosing inflammation of small and medium arteries of the hands and feet that nearly always occurs in heavy tobacco users. In the acute phase, the lumen holds a highly cellular thrombus with small microabscesses, sometimes with giant cells, and the inflammation spreads to the adjacent vein and nerve. The internal elastic lamina is usually preserved. Later the thrombus organizes and the artery, vein, and nerve are bound together by fibrosis. Nerve involvement helps explain his severe rest pain.
whyNot: Granulomas with giant cells centered on a fragmented internal elastic lamina describe giant cell arteritis, which affects older adults and the carotid branches and aorta.
Correct.

Atheroma is the lesion of atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease, usually in older patients with risk factors such as diabetes and high LDL. His age, normal lipids, and phlebitis point elsewhere.
Transmural fibrinoid necrosis with lesions of different ages is the pattern of polyarteritis nodosa. That disease does not involve veins and is not tied to smoking.

questions.stem: Angiography shows that the longest occlusion is in the artery that descends in the anterior compartment of the leg with the deep fibular nerve. Flow in which of the following arteries is most directly reduced as a result?
options: Posterior tibial artery
Medial plantar artery
Fibular artery
Dorsalis pedis artery
approach: Identify the occluded vessel: the artery of the anterior compartment, running with the deep fibular nerve, is the anterior tibial artery.
Follow it distally: it crosses the front of the ankle and continues on the dorsum of the foot.
Its continuation is the dorsalis pedis artery.
questions.why: The popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk. The anterior tibial artery passes into the anterior compartment, runs down with the deep fibular nerve, and crosses the front of the ankle midway between the malleoli. On the dorsum of the foot it continues as the dorsalis pedis artery, whose pulse is felt just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. An occlusion of the anterior tibial artery therefore removes direct flow to the dorsalis pedis.
whyNot: The posterior tibial artery is a branch of the tibioperoneal trunk in the posterior compartment. It runs with the tibial nerve and is felt behind the medial malleolus.
The medial plantar artery is a terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery in the sole, so it lies in a different arterial line.
The fibular artery also comes from the tibioperoneal trunk and runs in the posterior compartment near the fibula. It is not downstream of the anterior tibial artery.
Correct.

topics: Arteries of the leg and foot

questions.stem: One segment of a tibial artery has its radius reduced by half by thrombus and wall inflammation. If the pressure difference across that segment and blood viscosity remain constant, which of the following best approximates flow through the segment compared with baseline?
options: About 6 percent of baseline
About 12 percent of baseline
About 25 percent of baseline
About 50 percent of baseline
approach: Name the law: Poiseuille's law says resistance is inversely proportional to the radius to the fourth power.
Halving the radius gives (1/2) to the fourth power, which is 1/16.
Resistance rises 16-fold, so flow at the same pressure difference falls to 1/16, about 6 percent.
questions.why: By Poiseuille's law, flow equals the pressure difference times pi times the radius to the fourth power, divided by 8 times viscosity times length. Because radius enters to the fourth power, halving it raises resistance 16-fold. With the same pressure difference, flow falls to 1/16 of baseline, which is about 6 percent. This steep relationship is why modest narrowing of small distal arteries can leave toes without enough blood at rest.
whyNot: Correct.
About 12 percent (1/8) would follow if flow depended on the radius cubed. Poiseuille's law uses the fourth power.
About 25 percent (1/4) would follow if flow depended on cross-sectional area (radius squared). That underestimates the effect of narrowing on resistance.
About 50 percent would follow if flow changed in direct proportion to radius. Resistance depends far more steeply on radius than that.

questions.stem: His carboxyhemoglobin concentration is 8 percent (less than 2 percent in nonsmokers). Which of the following best describes how carbon monoxide further reduces oxygen delivery to his ischemic toes?
options: It oxidizes heme iron to the ferric form, producing methemoglobin
It shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve to the right, so oxygen unloads too early
It takes up heme sites and shifts the curve left, so less oxygen unloads
It lowers the dissolved oxygen in plasma, reducing the arterial PO2
approach: Key fact: carbon monoxide binds the iron of heme with an affinity about 200 times or more that of oxygen.
Bound CO lowers oxygen content by taking heme sites.
It also makes the remaining heme groups hold oxygen more tightly (a left shift), so less oxygen is released in tissues.
questions.why: Carbon monoxide binds ferrous heme far more tightly than oxygen does, so each CO molecule takes a site that oxygen could have used, lowering oxygen content. CO also changes the shape of the hemoglobin molecule so the remaining heme groups hold their oxygen more tightly, shifting the dissociation curve to the left. Tissues with already poor flow, such as his toes, then get even less oxygen. The arterial PO2 stays normal, because it reflects only dissolved oxygen.
whyNot: Oxidizing heme iron to the ferric (Fe3+) form produces methemoglobin, as with nitrites or dapsone. Carbon monoxide binds ferrous (Fe2+) heme without oxidizing it.
A right shift helps oxygen unload in tissues. Carbon monoxide shifts the curve in the opposite direction.
Correct.
The arterial PO2 depends on alveolar oxygen and lung function, which carbon monoxide does not change. Oxygen content falls because hemoglobin sites are occupied.

dx: Polyarteritis nodosa associated with hepatitis B
case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of fever, myalgias, and a 6-kg weight loss. For 3 weeks he has had crampy abdominal pain that begins about 30 minutes after meals. One week ago he developed numbness of the left ring and little fingers, and yesterday he awoke with a right foot drop. Blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg; 1 year ago it was 124/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows tender erythematous nodules and livedo reticularis over both legs. Serum creatinine concentration is 1.9 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urinalysis shows mild proteinuria with no red blood cell casts. Hepatitis B surface antigen is positive, and ANCA is negative. A chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Angiography shows multiple small aneurysms and segmental narrowing of the renal and mesenteric arteries. Diagnosis: polyarteritis nodosa associated with hepatitis B.

questions.stem: His arterial injury is attributed to a viral protein circulating in his blood. Which of the following immune mechanisms best explains the damage to his arteries?
options: IgE bound to mast cells triggers histamine release within the vessel wall
Antibodies bind antigens fixed on the surface of normal endothelial cells
Sensitized T cells form granulomas around viral antigen in the arterial media
Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in vessel walls and activate complement
approach: Key clue: hepatitis B surface antigen circulates in large amounts in his blood.
Soluble antigen plus antibody forms circulating immune complexes.
Complexes that lodge in vessel walls fix complement and recruit neutrophils: type III hypersensitivity.
questions.why: In hepatitis B-associated polyarteritis nodosa, circulating hepatitis B surface antigen combines with antibody to form immune complexes. These deposit in the walls of medium-sized arteries, activate complement, and draw in neutrophils, whose enzymes and oxidants cause fibrinoid necrosis. This is type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity. The weakened wall then forms the small aneurysms and narrowings seen on his angiogram.
whyNot: IgE on mast cells is type I hypersensitivity, which causes allergy and anaphylaxis. It does not cause necrotizing arteritis.
Antibody against an antigen fixed on cells or matrix is type II hypersensitivity, as in anti-glomerular basement membrane disease. Here the antigen circulates in the blood.
T cell granulomas are type IV hypersensitivity, the mechanism of giant cell arteritis. Polyarteritis nodosa shows neutrophils and fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas.
Correct.

questions.stem: Three years ago, after donating blood, he was told that he tested positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. Today, tests for IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen and for antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen are negative. Which of the following best describes the status of his hepatitis B infection?
options: Acute infection in its early phase
Chronic infection
Window period of a resolving infection
Past infection with lasting immunity
approach: Key clue: surface antigen has been present for years, far longer than 6 months.
IgM anti-core is a marker of recent infection, and it is negative.
Persistent surface antigen without anti-surface antibody means chronic infection.
questions.why: Hepatitis B surface antigen that persists for more than 6 months defines chronic infection. IgM antibody to core antigen appears in acute infection and fades over months, so a negative result fits long-standing infection. Antibody to surface antigen appears when the infection clears or after vaccination, and he has none. Ongoing antigen production in chronic infection supplies the antigen for the immune complexes in his arteries.
whyNot: Acute infection would show IgM antibody to core antigen, and surface antigen would not have been present 3 years ago.
Correct.
In the window period surface antigen has already disappeared and antibody to surface antigen has not yet appeared, with IgM anti-core as the main marker. His surface antigen is positive.
Past infection with immunity shows antibody to surface antigen and IgG anti-core, with no surface antigen in the blood.

questions.stem: His postprandial abdominal pain is caused by narrowing of the artery that supplies the jejunum and ileum. This artery arises from which of the following locations?
options: Anterior aorta at about the T12 vertebra
Anterior aorta at about the L1 vertebra
Lateral aorta at about the L1 to L2 vertebrae
Anterior aorta at about the L3 vertebra
approach: Identify the artery: the jejunum and ileum are midgut, supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
Recall the unpaired anterior branches of the abdominal aorta and their levels: celiac trunk T12, superior mesenteric L1, inferior mesenteric L3.
The superior mesenteric artery leaves the front of the aorta at about L1.
questions.why: The jejunum and ileum are midgut structures supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. It arises from the anterior surface of the abdominal aorta at about the L1 vertebral level, just below the celiac trunk, and passes behind the neck of the pancreas. Narrowing of its branches limits the increase in intestinal blood flow that normally follows a meal, which causes postprandial pain and food avoidance with weight loss, a pattern called intestinal angina.
whyNot: About T12 is the level of the celiac trunk, which supplies the foregut (stomach, liver, spleen, and proximal duodenum).
Correct.
Paired lateral branches at about L1 to L2 are the renal arteries. They are also often involved in polyarteritis nodosa, but they do not supply the small bowel.
About L3 is the level of the inferior mesenteric artery, which supplies the hindgut from the distal transverse colon to the upper rectum.

questions.stem: His blood pressure has increased as aneurysms and stenoses have developed in his renal arteries. Which of the following is the initiating event in this increase in blood pressure?
options: Juxtaglomerular cells sense a lower afferent arteriolar pressure and release renin
Macula densa cells sense a rise in tubular sodium chloride and trigger renin release
Atrial myocytes release natriuretic peptide in response to a larger blood volume
Carotid baroreceptors increase their firing and withdraw sympathetic tone
approach: Key clue: narrowed renal arteries lower the pressure reaching the glomeruli.
Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole act as pressure sensors and release renin when pressure falls.
Renin starts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which raises vascular resistance and sodium retention.
questions.why: Narrowing of renal arteries lowers the pressure in the afferent arterioles downstream. The juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole wall sense this lower stretch and release renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which angiotensin-converting enzyme turns into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles and stimulates aldosterone release, so sodium retention and vasoconstriction raise systemic blood pressure. This renovascular hypertension is common in polyarteritis nodosa.
whyNot: Correct.
A fall in sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa stimulates renin release. A rise in sodium chloride delivery suppresses renin.
Atrial natriuretic peptide promotes sodium excretion and vasodilation, so it lowers blood pressure.
Increased baroreceptor firing withdraws sympathetic tone, which lowers blood pressure. It is a response to high pressure, not its cause.

dx: Kawasaki disease with coronary artery dilation
case: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever for 6 days and marked irritability. His temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F). Physical examination shows bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection with limbal sparing, red cracked lips, and a strawberry tongue. There is a polymorphous erythematous rash over the trunk, erythema and edema of the hands and feet, and a single firm 2-cm left cervical lymph node. Laboratory studies show a C-reactive protein concentration of 110 mg/L (less than 10) and a leukocyte count of 19,600/µL (about 6,000 to 17,000 at his age). A rapid streptococcal antigen test and throat culture are negative. Echocardiography shows dilation of the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery. Diagnosis: Kawasaki disease.

questions.stem: Kawasaki disease targets medium-sized muscular arteries such as the coronary arteries. Histologic examination of a normal segment of his left anterior descending artery is most likely to show which of the following?
options: A smooth muscle media bounded by a distinct internal elastic lamina
A media built mostly of many fenestrated elastic lamellae
A thin media, wide lumen, and valves formed by folds of intima
Endothelium with fenestrations and a basal lamina, with no media at all
approach: Classify the vessel: coronary arteries are medium-sized muscular (distributing) arteries.
Recall the muscular artery wall: a thick media of smooth muscle between a prominent internal elastic lamina and an external elastic lamina.
Rule out the elastic artery, vein, and capillary patterns.
questions.why: Muscular arteries, such as the coronary, renal, and mesenteric arteries, have a media made mostly of layered smooth muscle. A distinct, wavy internal elastic lamina separates the intima from the media, and an external elastic lamina often marks the outer edge of the media. In Kawasaki disease, inflammation damages this smooth muscle and elastic tissue, and the weakened segment balloons into an aneurysm.
whyNot: Correct.
Many fenestrated elastic lamellae in the media mark an elastic (conducting) artery such as the aorta or pulmonary trunk. Kawasaki disease usually spares these.
A thin media, a wide lumen, and valves describe a medium-sized vein, especially in the limbs.
Endothelium with pores (fenestrations) on a basal lamina describes a fenestrated capillary, found in places such as the kidney and endocrine glands.

questions.stem: Scarlet fever was considered in the differential diagnosis because it can also cause a red tongue, rash, and later desquamation. The rash of scarlet fever is caused by a streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin that acts as a superantigen. Which of the following best describes how a superantigen activates T lymphocytes?
options: It is processed and presented in the MHC class II groove like a normal peptide
It cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine
It binds CD14 and TLR4 on macrophages in the same way as endotoxin
It links MHC class II to the T cell receptor beta chain outside the groove
approach: Identify the toxin: streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin A of Streptococcus pyogenes is a superantigen.
A superantigen skips antigen processing and binds the outside of MHC class II and the variable region of the T cell receptor beta chain.
Because many T cells share beta chain variable regions, a huge number are activated at once, releasing large amounts of cytokines.
questions.why: A normal peptide antigen is processed, loaded into the groove of an MHC molecule, and recognized only by the rare T cell clones whose receptors fit it. A superantigen is not processed. It binds intact to the outer surface of MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells and to the variable region of the T cell receptor beta chain. This links any T cell with a matching beta chain, activating a large fraction of all T cells. The surge of cytokines such as IL-2, interferon gamma, and TNF causes fever, rash, and, with toxic shock toxins, shock.
whyNot: Processing and presentation in the MHC groove is how conventional peptide antigens work. Only a tiny fraction of T cells respond to any one peptide.
Cross-linking IgE on mast cells and basophils is type I hypersensitivity, triggered by allergens, not streptococcal toxins.
CD14 and TLR4 recognize lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) from gram-negative bacteria and activate innate immunity. Streptococci are gram-positive and lack lipopolysaccharide.
Correct.

questions.stem: Over the next 2 weeks, the dilated segment enlarges into an aneurysm with an internal diameter 3 times that of the normal segment just upstream. Total blood flow through the artery is unchanged. Which of the following best describes the mean blood velocity in the aneurysm compared with the velocity upstream?
options: About one ninth as fast
About one third as fast
About the same as upstream
About three times as fast
approach: Apply the continuity principle: flow equals velocity times cross-sectional area, and flow is the same in both segments.
Area depends on the diameter squared, so tripling the diameter makes the area 9 times larger.
Velocity falls to 1/9, and slow flow in the aneurysm favors thrombus formation.
questions.why: When the same volume of blood per minute passes through segments in series, flow equals velocity times cross-sectional area in each segment. Cross-sectional area depends on the radius (or diameter) squared, so a 3-fold wider lumen has 9 times the area. Average velocity there drops to about one ninth of the upstream value. Slow, swirling flow in the aneurysm, together with injured endothelium and the high platelet counts of later Kawasaki disease, promotes thrombus that can block the artery and cause myocardial infarction.
whyNot: Correct.
One third as fast would be true if velocity depended on diameter directly. Area, and so velocity, depends on diameter squared.
Velocity stays the same only if the cross-sectional area is unchanged. Here the area is much larger.
Velocity rises, not falls, where a vessel narrows. Three times faster would fit a segment whose area was one third of normal.

questions.stem: In the third week of illness, the skin of his fingertips and toes begins to desquamate. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely at this stage?
options: Positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)
Rising antistreptolysin O titer
Platelet count well above the reference range
Low complement C3 and C4 levels
approach: Place him on the timeline: peeling of the fingers and toes marks the subacute phase, about weeks 2 to 4.
Recall the hallmark laboratory change of this phase: reactive thrombocytosis.
Rule out markers of other diseases: ANCA vasculitis, streptococcal infection, and immune complex disease.
questions.why: Kawasaki disease runs in phases. In the acute febrile phase, platelet counts are usually normal. In the subacute phase, about weeks 2 to 4, the fingers and toes peel and the platelet count rises, often to 500,000 to more than 1,000,000/µL (reference about 150,000 to 450,000). Platelet counts then fall back toward normal during convalescence. The high platelet count adds to the risk of thrombosis inside coronary aneurysms in this phase.
whyNot: ANCA is a marker of small-vessel vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. It is negative in Kawasaki disease.
A rising antistreptolysin O titer points to a recent Streptococcus pyogenes infection, as in rheumatic fever. His streptococcal tests were negative.
Correct.
Low C3 and C4 suggest complement consumption by immune complexes, as in lupus or cryoglobulinemia. Complement is not low in Kawasaki disease.

dx: Multifocal infantile hemangiomas with liver involvement
case: A 10-week-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. She was born at 31 weeks' gestation. Two weeks after birth, her parents noticed small red marks on her scalp, back, and right thigh, which have since grown rapidly. She is feeding well and gaining weight. Physical examination shows seven bright red, raised, lobulated lesions 0.5 to 2 cm in diameter that partially blanch with pressure. Because she has five or more cutaneous lesions, abdominal ultrasonography is performed and shows several small, well-defined, highly vascular lesions scattered throughout the liver. Diagnosis: multifocal infantile hemangiomas of the skin with liver involvement.

questions.stem: The skin lesions consist of tightly packed, capillary-sized channels lined by plump endothelial cells. In a normal continuous capillary, which of the following cells surrounds the endothelium and lies within the same basal lamina?
options: Smooth muscle cell
Fibroblast
Pericyte
Myoepithelial cell
approach: Key clue: the channels are capillary-sized, so compare them with the normal capillary wall.
A capillary wall has endothelium, a basal lamina, and scattered contractile cells with long processes.
These cells, enclosed by the endothelial basal lamina, are pericytes.
questions.why: A continuous capillary is a tube of endothelial cells joined by tight junctions and resting on a basal lamina. Pericytes wrap their long processes around the endothelium and sit inside a split in that basal lamina. They have contractile proteins, help stabilize the vessel, and can give rise to smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts after injury. Proliferating infantile hemangiomas contain both endothelial cells and pericytes arranged in capillary-sized lobules.
whyNot: Smooth muscle cells form the media of arteries, arterioles, and veins. Capillaries have no muscular media.
Fibroblasts lie in the surrounding connective tissue outside the basal lamina and do not wrap the endothelium.
Correct.
Myoepithelial cells wrap glandular secretory units, such as sweat and breast glands, not blood vessels.

questions.stem: At 14 weeks of age, the liver lesions have increased in size and number. Her serum TSH concentration is now increased and her free T4 concentration decreased for her age, although her newborn thyroid screen was normal. An enzyme produced by the hemangioma tissue is inactivating thyroid hormone faster than her thyroid gland can replace it. Which of the following reactions does this enzyme catalyze?
options: Removing an inner-ring iodine, converting T4 to reverse T3
Removing an outer-ring iodine, converting T4 into active T3
Blocking iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter
Blocking thyroid peroxidase coupling of iodotyrosines
approach: Key clue: normal newborn screen, then low free T4 with high TSH once large liver hemangiomas appear, so the hormone is being destroyed outside the thyroid.
Hemangioma tissue can express type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase.
Type 3 deiodinase removes an inner-ring iodine, turning T4 into inactive reverse T3 (and T3 into inactive T2).
questions.why: Infantile hemangiomas, especially large or numerous liver lesions, can express high levels of type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase. This enzyme removes an iodine from the inner ring of thyroid hormone, converting T4 into inactive reverse T3 and T3 into inactive T2. When the lesions break down hormone faster than the thyroid can make it, free T4 falls and TSH rises. This is called consumptive hypothyroidism, and it matters in infancy because thyroid hormone is needed for brain development.
whyNot: Correct.
Removing an outer-ring iodine is done by type 1 and type 2 deiodinases and activates the hormone by making T3. It would not lower her thyroid hormone activity.
Blocking the sodium-iodide symporter reduces hormone synthesis within the gland, as perchlorate or thiocyanate can. The problem here is breakdown of hormone outside the thyroid.
Blocking thyroid peroxidase reduces hormone synthesis within the gland, as thionamide drugs do. Her gland works normally, as shown by her normal newborn screen.

questions.stem: Over the next month the liver lesions enlarge. Her pulse is 180/min (about 100 to 160 at her age). Physical examination shows bounding pulses, a wide pulse pressure, and hepatomegaly. Which of the following is the initiating change in this high-output state?
options: Higher systemic vascular resistance from a surge of catecholamine release
Lower contractility that reduces stroke volume and causes reflex tachycardia
Reduced venous return as the enlarged liver presses on the vena cava
Shunting through the lesions that lowers systemic vascular resistance
approach: Key clues: bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, and tachycardia point to high cardiac output with low resistance.
Large vascular liver lesions act as low-resistance shunts between arteries and veins.
Lower systemic vascular resistance lowers diastolic pressure and increases venous return, so the heart must pump more blood each minute.
questions.why: Large or numerous liver hemangiomas can contain arteriovenous and portovenous shunts. Blood takes this low-resistance path, so systemic vascular resistance falls. Diastolic pressure drops, which widens the pulse pressure and makes pulses bounding. More blood returns quickly to the heart, and cardiac output rises with tachycardia to keep arterial pressure up. If the demand outstrips the heart, she develops high-output heart failure with an enlarged liver.
whyNot: Higher systemic vascular resistance would narrow the pulse pressure and lower cardiac output. Her findings show the opposite.
Lower contractility reduces stroke volume and cardiac output. It would give weak pulses and a narrow pulse pressure, not bounding pulses with a wide pulse pressure.
Reduced venous return lowers cardiac output by the Frank-Starling mechanism. A high-output state needs more venous return, not less.
Correct.

topics: Systemic vascular resistance and pulse pressure

questions.stem: Her parents ask what the skin lesions will do over time if they cause no complications. Which of the following is the most likely course?
options: Growth in proportion to her body throughout life, without any regression
More growth for a few months, then slow regression over several years
Steady shrinking that is complete within a few more weeks
Slow conversion into angiosarcoma during early childhood
approach: Key clues: lesions absent at birth, appeared in the first weeks, and are growing fast.
This is the natural history of infantile hemangioma: rapid growth in early infancy, then slow involution.
Rule out the patterns of vascular malformations and malignant vascular tumors.
questions.why: Infantile hemangiomas are absent or faint at birth and appear in the first weeks of life. Most of their growth happens in the first 3 to 5 months. Growth then slows and stops, and the lesions involute slowly over several years, with most regression finished by about age 4. Some leave behind thin, wrinkled skin, fibrofatty tissue, or telangiectasias. Female sex and preterm birth, both present here, are known risk factors.
whyNot: Growth in proportion to the child with no regression describes a vascular malformation, such as a capillary malformation (port-wine stain), which is present at birth.
Correct.
Infantile hemangiomas do not disappear within weeks. Involution takes years.
Infantile hemangiomas are benign and do not turn into angiosarcoma. Angiosarcoma is a rare malignant tumor, usually of older adults.
